nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the ghost story and the psychological weird
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of 'The Beckoning Fair One', the greatest English ghost story of the century.
biography: Born George Oliver Onions at Bradford on 13 November 1873; he studied art in London and Paris, worked as a commercial artist, and published The Compleat Bachelor (1901), Widdershins (1911) and some forty novels. He changed his name to George Oliver in 1918 and died in Aberystwyth on 9 April 1961.
literary_profile: Oliver Onions wrote 'The Beckoning Fair One', the greatest English ghost story of the century and one of the finest supernatural tales ever written: Widdershins is the central collection of the modern psychological ghost story, and his work stands with M. R. James and Blackwood at the summit of the English weird tale.
stylistic_characteristics: The psychological ghost story of the obsessive; the haunted flat and the haunted artist; the slow, exact, cumulative narration; the ambiguity of the supernatural; the plain, dry, careful prose.
intellectual_concerns: The absurd, the void; art versus life, and the romance of the artist; sexuality, the new psychology; myth, ritual, and the primitive imagination.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the allegory of the Dorset village
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of Mr Weston's Good Wine, one of the strangest and finest English novels of the century.
biography: Born Theodore Francis Powys at Shirley, Derbyshire, on 17 December 1875, the brother of John Cowper and Llewelyn Powys; he lived as a farmer and then in the Dorset village of East Chaldon, and published The Soliloquy of a Hermit (1916), Black Bryony (1923), Mark Only (1924), Mr Tasker's Gods (1925) and Mr Weston's Good Wine (1927). He died at Mappowder, Dorset, on 27 November 1953.
literary_profile: T. F. Powys wrote Mr Weston's Good Wine, one of the strangest and finest English novels of the century and the great English allegory of the twentieth century: his parable of the wine merchant who is God visiting a Dorset village made him the central English allegorist of the period.
stylistic_characteristics: The allegory in a village setting; the parable of the divine visitor; the comic and the terrible side by side; the flat, biblical, understated prose; the Dorset village as the stage of the cosmic.
intellectual_concerns: Religion, doubt, and the post-war faith; the countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; the absurd, the void; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy.
historical_significance: T. F. Powys wrote Mr Weston's Good Wine, one of the strangest and finest English novels of the century: his parable of the wine merchant who is God visiting a Dorset village made him the central English allegorist of the period.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the sociology of race and the double consciousness
literary_identity: Sociologist, historian, editor and activist; the founder of the NAACP and the greatest Black American intellectual of the century.
biography: Born William Edward Burghardt Du Bois in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, on 23 February 1868; he took a doctorate at Harvard, taught at Atlanta University, and published The Souls of Black Folk in 1903. He edited The Crisis from 1910, founded the Niagara Movement and the NAACP, wrote Black Reconstruction (1935) and moved to Ghana, where he died in Accra on 27 August 1963.

stylistic_characteristics: The essay and the sociological survey side by side; the spiritual and the statistic; the double consciousness of the Black American; the plain, formal, prophetic prose; the direct address to the white reader.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line, and the New Negro; slavery, emancipation, and the unfinished Reconstruction; democracy, individualism, and the American experiment; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent.
historical_significance: W. E. B. Du Bois was the greatest Black American intellectual of the century and the founder of the sociology of race: The Souls of Black Folk created the modern literature of the colour line and gave the century its central idea of double consciousness.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Black novel and the sermon in verse
literary_identity: Poet, novelist, critic and civil-rights leader; the first Black executive secretary of the NAACP and the author of The Autobiography of an Ex-Coloured Man.
biography: Born James William Johnson in Jacksonville, Florida, on 17 June 1871; he was a schoolteacher, a lawyer and a songwriter, wrote the lyrics of 'Lift Every Voice and Sing', and served as US consul in Venezuela and Nicaragua. The Autobiography of an Ex-Coloured Man (1912), God's Trombones (1927) and Black Manhattan (1930) followed, with his leadership of the NAACP. He died in Wiscasset, Maine, on 26 June 1938.

stylistic_characteristics: The first-person passing narrative; the sermon in free verse; the anonymity and the confession; the folk sermon and the spiritual; the plain, formal, dignified prose and the rhetorical verse.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line, and the New Negro; slavery, emancipation, and the unfinished Reconstruction; religion, doubt, and the post-war faith; the American city, the machine, and the moneyed metropolis.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the passing narrative and the Harlem Renaissance novel
literary_identity: Novelist and nurse; the finest novelist of the Harlem Renaissance and the author of Passing and Quicksand.
biography: Born Nella Marian Larsen in Chicago on 13 April 1891, the daughter of a Danish mother and a Black West Indian father; she trained as a nurse and worked as a librarian in Harlem, and published Quicksand in 1928 and Passing in 1929. She was the first Black woman to win a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1930, published little afterwards, and died in New York on 30 March 1964.
literary_profile: Nella Larsen was the finest novelist of the Harlem Renaissance: Quicksand and Passing are the two great novels of the movement, and Passing is the central text of the American literature of racial passing and of the Black woman's interior life.
stylistic_characteristics: The short novel of the interior life; the passing narrative of racial ambiguity; the restrained, exact, ironic prose; the party and the Harlem salon; the refusal of a moral conclusion.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line, and the New Negro; sexuality, the new psychology; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Black middle-class novel and the Harlem editorship
literary_identity: Novelist, poet and editor; the literary editor of The Crisis and the midwife of the Harlem Renaissance.
biography: Born Jessie Redmon Fauset in Camden County, New Jersey, on 27 April 1882; she was the first Black woman to graduate from Cornell, taught French in Washington and New York, and edited The Crisis from 1919 to 1926, publishing the writers of the Harlem Renaissance. There Is Confusion (1924), Plum Bun (1928), The Chinaberry Tree (1931) and Comedy: American Style (1933) followed. She died in Philadelphia on 30 April 1961.
literary_profile: Jessie Fauset was the literary editor of The Crisis and the midwife of the Harlem Renaissance: she published the movement's writers, and her four novels of the Black middle class created the fiction of Black bourgeois life and the Black woman's ambition.
stylistic_characteristics: The novel of the Black middle class; the romance and the social comedy; the exact detail of the Black professional household; the plain, formal, realistic prose; the argument for the ordinary dignity of Black life.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line, and the New Negro; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Black historical novel and the Harlem Renaissance
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and librarian; the author of God Sends Sunday and Black Thunder, and the great Black historical novelist of the Renaissance.
biography: Born Arna Wendell Bontemps in Alexandria, Louisiana, on 13 October 1902; he was raised in California, taught in Harlem, and published God Sends Sunday (1931), Black Thunder (1936) and Drums at Dusk (1939), with the poetry of Personals (1963) and the anthology The Poetry of the Negro (1949, with Langston Hughes). He was librarian at Fisk University and died in Nashville on 4 June 1973.
literary_profile: Arna Bontemps was the great Black historical novelist of the Harlem Renaissance: Black Thunder is the finest American novel of the slave rebellion, God Sends Sunday created the Black sporting novel, and his anthologies with Langston Hughes preserved the poetry of the movement.
stylistic_characteristics: The historical novel of the slave South; the dialect and the folk song; the rebellion and the hanging; the plain, spare, documentary prose; the ballad and the spiritual in the texture.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery, emancipation, and the unfinished Reconstruction; race, the colour line, and the New Negro; religion, doubt, and the post-war faith; the American wilderness and the myth of the forest.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Black folk poetry and the ballad
literary_identity: Poet, critic and teacher; the finest Black poet of the folk tradition in America and the author of Southern Road.
biography: Born Sterling Allen Brown in Washington, D.C., on 1 May 1901; he was educated at Dunbar High School, Williams College and Harvard, and taught at Howard University from 1929, where he trained a generation of Black writers. Southern Road (1932) and the criticism collected in Negro Poetry and Drama (1937) followed. He died in Washington on 13 January 1989.
